Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> National COP31: Disability community gets audience with AGN Chair for inclusivity in climate negotiation process Source : Kofi Adu Domfeh 15 November 2026 8:24am ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
When sudden floodwaters tore through the streets of Accra last June, the devastation left behind was measured not only in damaged infrastructure, but in broken lives and lost independence.
For many residents with disabilities, the rising waters swept away their essential assistive devices, including wheelchairs and crutches, shattering their livelihoods in a matter of hours.
As climate-induced extreme weather events intensify across the globe, persons with disabilities find themselves at the acute epicenter of vulnerability. Yet, despite bearing the heaviest burden of global warming, their voices remain largely excluded from the formal halls of international climate diplomacy.
Now, a growing global movement led by African disability advocates and backed by the African Group of Negotiators (AGN) is fighting to change that narrative at the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye.
"Climate change affects all of us, but affects some more than others, and those some are persons with disabilities," explains Peter Anoma-Kodie, Executive Director of the Ghana Federation of Disability Organizations.
Anoma-Kodie paints a harrowing picture of what climate vulnerability looks like on the ground. During severe environmental events, physical limitations leave persons with disabilities with fewer escape options.
"When it comes to running or swimming, we don't have those skills," Anoma-Kodie points out. "So when there's a change, and there's a flood or drought, we are the ones who suffer most often."
The hazards extend far beyond sudden floods. Slow-onset climate impacts, such as prolonged heatwaves and soaring global temperatures, inflict severe health crises on specific disability communities. In tropical regions, extreme heat exposure poses a life-threatening risk to persons with albinism, triggering sharp spikes in skin cancer and devastating dermatological conditions.
The peril faced by persons with disabilities during environmental catastrophes is compounded by a systemic lack of accessible infrastructure and communication. Disaster management protocols routinely overlook the basic accessibility needs of disabled populations.
"The most challenging part is that we are not able to get early warnings in accessible formats," Anoma-Kodie emphasizes. "During disasters, we don't get information in accessible formats in terms of sign language or live captions. We don't get those things, and after the disaster, it's the exact same story."
Without accessible early warnings, deaf individuals cannot hear emergency sirens or broadcasts, visually impaired individuals cannot read print evacuation notices, and mobility-impaired individuals are left trapped without accessible transport. This structural exclusion turns natural hazards into fatal disasters.
"That is why we think that we need to be at the table," Anoma-Kodie stresses. "So that we make sure that climate processes are all fully accessible to persons with disabilities."
Recognizing that policy change requires seat-at-the-table representation, disability leaders engaged in high-level diplomacy at COP31 to secure formal recognition within the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC).
A pivotal breakthrough occurred following a bilateral strategy session between the African disability community and the Chair of the African Group of Negotiators (AGN), Nana Dr. Antwi-Boasiako Amoah.
The delegation urged the AGN, a key negotiating bloc representing African countries, to champion the disability caucus's bid for official observer status and formal constituency recognition.
Nana Amoah pledged his full support to mobilize the African negotiating bloc behind the disability movement, committing to organize dedicated meetings between AGN delegates and disability representatives to expedite their recognition process.
"The chair was very optimistic," Anoma-Kodie recalled after the meeting. "He mentioned that he would do his best to organize a meeting for us with the AGN so that persons with disabilities can articulate their issues and influence the negotiation process to get our observer status as quickly as possible. He was very friendly and clearly dedicated to disability inclusion."
Globally, an estimated 1.3 billion people – 16 percent of the world’s population – live with disabilities. According to joint appeals from the International Disability Alliance (IDA) and regional forums including the African Disability Forum (ADF), ASEAN Disability Forum, European Disability Forum (EDF), and Latin American Network of NGOs (RIADIS), climate adaptation policies can only succeed if principles of universal design and accessibility are placed at their core.
Currently, the UNFCCC recognizes nine official constituencies, including Women and Gender, Youth, and Indigenous Peoples’ Organizations. These constituencies receive critical privileges: making plenary interventions, receiving advance drafting documents from the UNFCCC Secretariat, and collaborating directly in closed negotiating rounds.
Despite international human rights mandates, such as Article 4.3 of the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD), which obligates states to consult disabled populations, disability organizations still lack an official UNFCCC constituency status.
"If we are not sitting at the table, it means that we will not be able to articulate our issues," Anoma-Kodie warns. Official constituency status would grant disabled advocates equal standing to shape climate adaptation funds, disaster risk reduction frameworks, and Just Transition policies.
For advocates on the ground in Antalya and across Africa, disability inclusion in climate action is not a matter of charity; it is a fundamental human rights imperative.
"Climate change is a human rights issue," Anoma-Kodie declared in his takeaway from the climate summit. "If we don't act today, it means that we are denying other people the right to live tomorrow. This is a campaign that we all need to get involved in. We should have started yesterday, but today is not too late."
With the backing of the African Group of Negotiators, the disability bloc is pushing to turn UN pledges into binding, funded commitments. As negotiations continue, their message to world leaders is unambiguous: effective global climate solutions can only be built when the world's most vulnerable populations have a direct hand in shaping them.
